target: AG1’s claim that a national Election Day holiday would remove scheduling barriers that keep millions from voting.
objection: A federal holiday would not reliably solve the problem because most private employers are not required to give paid time off, especially in retail, food service, health care, and other hourly or essential jobs. Low-income workers in those sectors could still be scheduled during polling hours, so the holiday would not remove the barrier in the way the pro side claims.

target: AG2’s claim that many constrained workers would still be stuck working through polling hours even on a holiday.
objection: A national holiday would still change real schedules in ways that reduce the barrier: schools close, many businesses close or reduce hours, and employers often adjust shifts on federal holidays. So the objection that the holiday would fail unless it guaranteed paid leave for every private employer is too strong.

target: AG1’s rebuttal that school closures and broad holiday schedule changes would make voting easier for constrained workers.
objection: School closures and holiday schedule effects are not reliable enough to solve the barrier. A federal holiday does not force all schools or childcare providers to close, and many low-income workers in essential jobs can still be scheduled during polling hours, so the holiday still leaves the hardest-to-reach voters time-constrained.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday would still not create usable time for workers because they might remain scheduled.
objection: Even if some workers remain on shift, the holiday still meaningfully reduces the barrier because voters no longer have to sacrifice wages, risk attendance problems, or fit voting into a normal workday. A paid non-work day directly addresses the time constraint the other side highlights.

target: AG1’s claim that holiday effects would be widespread enough to give constrained workers usable time through school closures and employer adjustments.
objection: That assumption is too broad. Many private employers would still schedule workers, and lower traffic or school closures do not reliably help low-income workers who still must commute or cover childcare. So the holiday would not broadly remove the practical time barrier for the people who need relief most.

target: AG2’s claim that workers would still lack workable time because they are scheduled during polling hours.
objection: The key problem for many voters is that they cannot be away from work or school without losing wages or risking their job. A national holiday as a paid non-work day directly gives them the time they need, which addresses the constraint much more effectively than the other side suggests.

target: AG2’s claim that being scheduled for work means voting is still not feasible.
objection: Working on Election Day does not necessarily prevent voting, because the real barrier is finding a workable window. A holiday reduces that barrier by creating a day with different time pressures, shorter effective voting windows, and more opportunity to vote before or after shifts.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday creates enough workable time around shifts.
objection: A holiday does not ensure workers can actually get away from their shifts or that commuting and waiting time shrink enough to make voting feasible. Many low-income workers still face the same tradeoff between working, losing pay, or not being able to fit voting into the time they have.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status does not reduce the total time cost of voting.
objection: A holiday can reduce travel and coordination burdens: traffic and commuting friction are often lower, and more family or community members are off, making rides or supervision easier to arrange. That reduces the non-work time a constrained voter needs to spend in order to vote.

target: AG1’s claim that travel and coordination costs fall enough on a holiday to help low-income workers.
objection: Lower traffic and easier coordination are not dependable for shift workers. Essential workers still commute, and the people they rely on for rides or supervision may also be working. So the holiday does not reliably shrink travel or coordination time for the hardest-to-reach voters.

target: AG2’s claim that OECD holiday elections do not show a holiday can make voting workable.
objection: The fact that 27 of 36 OECD countries hold elections on weekends or holidays shows that such scheduling is a workable real-world approach. If holiday elections generally failed to help, so many comparable democracies would not use them.

target: AG1’s use of OECD countries as evidence that holiday elections work.
objection: International adoption does not prove the holiday itself solves U.S. scheduling problems, because other countries have different labor rules, stronger time-off protections, and more expansive early or absentee voting. The precedent may reflect those supporting institutions rather than the holiday being the crucial causal factor.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday does not reduce the time cost of voting enough to matter.
objection: A national holiday spreads voting demand over the day and across more available people, which can reduce peak congestion and waiting times. That shorter line time and more flexible timing can make voting workable even for workers who still have shifts.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday does not meaningfully shorten the voting process.
objection: Election operations are staffing-dependent, and a holiday can free more volunteers and workers to serve as poll workers, which can shorten lines and reduce the total time needed to vote. That makes the holiday more than a symbolic change.

target: AG1’s broader claim that a holiday by itself is a strong turnout reform.
objection: Holiday status mainly changes convenience, while turnout is often driven by deeper barriers like registration rules, administrative friction, and limited voting options. Research shows election holidays alone do not reliably raise turnout as much as direct access reforms do.

target: AG2’s claim that holiday status is only a weak convenience change.
objection: The holiday directly targets a major practical barrier: work and school schedules that keep millions from voting. It is not merely about attention; it gives people actual time off and reshapes the civic environment around voting.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday would function like a paid non-work day for schedule-constrained workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not require private employers to provide paid time off or stop scheduling workers. In sectors where low-income hourly and essential workers are concentrated, many employees would still have to work during voting hours, so the holiday would not reliably create the needed time.

target: AG2’s claim that a holiday is only a minor convenience tweak rather than a turnout reform.
objection: The real barrier for many voters is not motivation but time. A national holiday changes school schedules, workplace routines, and the broader availability of people and civic infrastructure, which directly increases the number of workable voting windows.

target: AG1’s claim that a paid non-school/non-work day would give schedule-constrained voters the needed time.
objection: That causal chain depends on a broad paid-day-off mechanism that federal holiday status does not guarantee. Private employers, especially in hourly sectors, can still schedule employees during polling hours, so the holiday does not reliably remove the core time barrier.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday only changes attention or symbolism.
objection: Election Day should be a holiday because it directly tackles the major practical barrier of work and school scheduling, creates real time for voting, and has broad public and international support, showing it is a workable turnout reform rather than a symbolic gesture.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday reliably reshapes routines enough to create usable voting time.
objection: A federal holiday does not guarantee that private employers will close or give paid time off. Many low-income workers in retail, food service, caregiving, logistics, and similar jobs can still be scheduled during voting hours, so the holiday does not reliably create usable time for them.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday does not meaningfully loosen work and attendance constraints.
objection: A non-school/non-work day substantially loosens those constraints because schools close, childcare pressure falls, and workplace routines shift. That creates workable voting windows even for many hourly and essential workers.

target: AG1’s claim that a federal holiday broadly creates paid non-work time and school/childcare availability.
objection: Federal holiday status does not require most private employers to close or provide paid leave, so many hourly and essential workers would still have to choose between voting and losing wages or facing attendance problems. That undercuts the claim that the holiday meaningfully creates usable time for the people most constrained.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is low-yield because it only changes convenience.
objection: The key barrier is workable time, not just convenience. A non-school/non-work day reduces commute friction, peak congestion, and line length, making voting substantially easier for people with rigid schedules.

target: AG1’s claim that a holiday broadly reduces time barriers for low-income workers.
objection: A federal holiday does not compel most private employers to close or provide paid time off, especially in industries with many shift workers. That means the very workers the policy is supposed to help may still face the same work-vs-voting tradeoff, including travel and waiting time.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is merely a weak convenience reform.
objection: The holiday directly removes a major scheduling barrier by giving people a non-school/non-work day, reshaping weekday routines, and reducing the time cost of voting. International precedent and broad public support reinforce that it is a workable turnout reform.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday substantially loosens work and attendance constraints for constrained voters.
objection: A federal holiday does not require most private employers to close or pay workers, so shift-based workers in retail, food service, health care, and similar sectors can still be scheduled during polling hours. Without guaranteed time off, the work-voting tradeoff remains for many low-income workers.

target: AG2’s claim that the holiday is only a low-yield convenience measure.
objection: The key barrier is workable time, and a non-school/non-work day substantially loosens work and attendance constraints. That helps people vote without sacrificing wages or obligations, making the reform high-yield rather than weak.

target: AG1’s claim that the holiday substantially loosens work and school constraints for those most affected.
objection: The argument assumes a federal holiday makes Election Day effectively non-work for the people who need it most, but private employers are not required to close or provide paid time off. Many hourly and essential workers will still be scheduled during voting hours, so the holiday does not reliably remove the core time tradeoff.
